paras: The lynching of Washington Ives was the hanging of a Black man near Natchez, Mississippi, on the night of June 16, 1888, after he was accused of attempting to assault a young woman. His body was found the next morning hanging from a tree with a card warning against rape, and no one was reported arrested. The Natchez wire report ran in papers from New York to Georgia, and the case later appeared on a year-end list of the "Victims of Judge Lynch."

According to the account the wire attributed to the coroner's inquest, Ives entered a house on Friday night, June 15, and attempted to assault a young woman. Her cries raised the alarm, and he escaped for the time being. Several briefs described the woman as white, and the Savannah text called her "a most estimable young lady"; she was not named.

Ives was later caught and, in the wire's words, "quietly lynched." Briefs dated the lynching to Saturday night, and a June 17 dispatch said it took place about three miles from Natchez "last night." At daylight on Sunday, June 17, his body was found hanging from a tree about three miles from the city. Attached to it was a card reading "Beware of Committing Rape," a wording other versions gave as "assault" or "outrage."

A coroner's inquest was held, and its findings about the alleged attempted assault became the substance of the wire story. No report of arrests, a grand jury inquiry or an inquest finding about the killers appears in the coverage. Mississippi papers reported that a second Black man, Spencer Collins, was hanged near Natchez on the Pine Ridge road the following night for a similar accusation, and state roundups counted two lynchings in Adams County that week.

The story reached the white press through a Natchez dispatch dated June 17, printed the next day by the New York Sun under "A Negro Lynched" and by the Savannah Morning News and the Washington Critic. The New York Evening World headed its version "He Was Hanged as a Warning." These texts repeated the inquest's version of the alleged crime as fact, and the Savannah text said the punishment "was swiftly and silently performed." Shorter weekly-summary briefs carried the case to Kentucky, Indiana, Wisconsin and Vermont papers over the next two weeks.

Mississippi weeklies wrote the name as "Inge" and gave the case a line each. The Copiah Signal called Inge and Collins "desperadoes" and wrote that their community "now breathes easier." The Greenville Times and the Chickasaw Messenger folded the Natchez killings into a count of three lynchings in the state that week, all of Black men accused of assaulting women. In December the case appeared in a year-end list of lynchings as "Washington Ives at Natchez, Miss.," dated June 17.

The victim's surname is "Ives" in the wire and out-of-state papers but "Inge" in the Southern Herald, the Brookhaven Leader and the Copiah Signal. The Brookhaven Leader reported that Inge and Collins were lynched together "the first of this week," while the Copiah Signal placed the two hangings on successive nights. The dated Natchez dispatches support the night of June 16 for Ives's death, though one summary brief gave "the 18th."

reader.title: Lynching of Washington Ives
bases: A Black man accused of attempted rape was found hanged from a tree near Natchez with a warning card on the body, and every report calls it a lynching (A1, A2, A5).

Ives was hanged by unnamed parties with no lawful authority after an accusation of attempted rape, with a card warning against rape attached to the body (A1, A2); no report gives the number of lynchers, but all describe a lynching rather than a lone killing (A1, A4, A14).

The Natchez wire report (A1, A2, A5) and separately worded Mississippi papers that spell the name 'Inge' (A8, A14, A20) agree that a Black man named Washington was lynched near Natchez for attempted rape that weekend.

accounts.label: Wire report (from the coroner's inquest)
accounts.gist: Ives entered a house Friday night and attempted to assault a young lady, escaped when she cried out, and was caught and 'quietly lynched'; his body was found Sunday morning with a warning card.

accounts.label: Mississippi weeklies
accounts.gist: Washington 'Inge' was lynched in Adams county for attempted rape; two papers add that Spencer Collins was lynched near Natchez the same week, the Copiah Signal placing Collins's hanging the night after Inge's.

framing.detail: Northern papers ran the Natchez wire under 'A Negro Lynched' or 'He Was Hanged as a Warning', presenting the inquest's account of the attempted assault as fact.

The Savannah text called the woman 'a most estimable young lady' and said the punishment was 'swiftly and silently performed'; the Copiah Signal called the hanged men 'desperadoes' and said the community 'breathes easier'.
Mississippi briefs and state roundups noted the lynching in a line, counting it among three lynchings in the state that week.

conflicts.note: The wire and all out-of-state papers say Ives; three Mississippi weeklies say Inge. Neither version is clearly better evidence; no Natchez paper was found.
